text: AI text detectors that show their work. DetectorScope turns a black-box AI text detector into one whose every prediction is a sum of named, validated features. It can tell you which properties of a text made it predict "AI" and where in the text they are located. Try our demo! 🤗 https://huggingface.co/spaces/liamdugan/detector-scope-demo Installation pip install detectorscope Example Usage from detectorscope import AuditableDetector # Load the AI detector detector = AuditableDetector . from_pretrained ( "liamdugan/detector-scope" ) # Run the AI detector on some input output = detector ( "Like I said, this is about accuracy, about speed, and about cost." ) # Print the results print ( output ) Detection(label='ai', p_ai=0.88, features=[ Feature(importance=+0.23, description='the word about used as a preposition'), Feature(importance=+0.14, description='repeated phrases or sequences in text'), Feature(importance=-0.05, description='conversational filler phrase like i said'), ...]) Using DetectorScope you can: The pipeline: SAEs on the detector's residual stream, a description and validation score per feature, a threshold on that score, and a sparse head over the features that pass. A DetectorScope detector is a concept bottleneck over interpretable sparse-autoencoder features: the language model's residual stream is encoded by SAEs, each feature gets a natural-language description that is validated against its own activations, and a sparse linear head over the validated features makes the decision. The prediction is therefore a sum of per-feature contributions, and every contribution has a description and a location in the text. F1 (COLING) and TPR at 5% FPR (RAID) against the interpretability threshold, in domain (grey) and out of domain (white). FT-Model+SAE matches the underlying neural detector even at thresholds of 0.7 and above. Across both benchmarks applying our auditable pipeline has minimal adverse effects on performance. The auditable detectors stay close to the fine-tuned black-box classifier they are built on. The full tables are in the paper . From PyPI, in a fresh environment: python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate pip install detectorscope From source, with the extras for the pipeline, the experiments and the demo: git clone https://github.com/google-deepmind/detectorscope && cd detectorscope pip install -e " .[all] " Usage Any released detector loads by its Hub id; the other settings of a repo are its branches. from detectorscope import AuditableDetector detector = AuditableDetector . from_pretrained ( "liamdugan/detector-scope-peer-review-gpt4o" ) detector = AuditableDetector . from_pretrained ( "liamdugan/detector-scope" , revision = "base-sae" ) detector(text) returns a Detection with label , p_ai , logit , bias and features , every feature active in the text with a non-zero effect, largest first. importance is how much the logit falls if the feature is silenced, and logit == bias + sum(importances) . A list of texts returns a list. Set return_highlights=True to see where each feature is localized within the text: output = detector ( text , return_highlights = True ) output . tokens # the text as tokens output . features [ 0 ]. highlights # [(token index, activation), ...] You can use the tau parameter to control the tradeoff between interpretability and accuracy. Every feature has an auto-interpretation score, how well its description predicts where it fires, and tau is the score a feature must reach before the head is allowed to use it. A higher tau gives the head fewer, better-described features, so every item of evidence it reports is one you can read and check, at some cost in accuracy. A lower tau admits more features, including ones whose descriptions are loose, and the detector gets more accurate and less legible. The default is 0.85. detector = AuditableDetector . from_pretrained ( "liamdugan/detector-scope" , tau = 0.95 ) tau runs from 0.00 (every feature) to 0.95 in steps of 0.05, and each branch carries a head at every step, so changing it downloads nothing. It can also be set per call, which is the easiest way to compare the same text at several settings: output = detector ( text , tau = 0.50 ) # more features, higher accuracy output = detector ( text , tau = 0.95 ) # the few best-described features detector . heads # every (head, tau) pair the repo holds head="xgboost" , on from_pretrained or on the call, selects the gradient-boosted head at the same tau instead of the logistic-regression one. We provide the following model collections for download via Huggingface : Each repo holds the paper's three settings as branches. ft-model-sae fine-tunes Gemma-2-2b as a classifier and fine-tunes the SAEs on it; ft-sae keeps the unmodified Gemma-2-2b and fine-tunes only the SAEs; base-sae keeps both the unmodified Gemma-2-2b and the unmodified Gemma Scope SAEs. main is the setting that performed best on each domain: ft-sae for the open domain, ft-model-sae for peer reviews. Every branch bundles its language model, so nothing else is downloaded and no licence gate is involved. The defaults are set by hand: the logistic-regression head over features whose auto-interpretation score is at least 0.85, with the decision threshold fixed on the development split. Each branch also carries the XGBoost head and both heads at every other threshold. The pipeline that builds a detector is the package's stages, run as python -m detectorscope.<stage> : finetune (the classifier), train_sae (SAEs on its residual stream), data.extract and data.process (per-token activations, per-document caches, log-odds ratios, feature statistics), autointerpret (descriptions and their validation, through Gemini; set GEMINI_API_KEY ), model.detectors.heads.training.train_logreg / train_xgboost (the heads) and evaluate . Stages 0 to 2 need a GPU; the rest runs on CPUs. The experiments are four scripts under scripts/ : hparam_sweep.py (the SGD + L1 grid search), counterfactual_ablation.py (zero-ablation vs. targeted paraphrase of single features), paraphrase_ablation.py (the feature-guided paraphrase attack) and regex_recall_ablation.py (regex recall of the descriptions). Every figure and table of the paper comes from scripts/visualization/analysis.ipynb , and --help on any script lists its arguments. demo/ is the Gradio app, which runs locally with python demo/app.py and as the Hugging Face Space; scripts/huggingface_hub/ exports the detectors to the Hub and publishes the Space. @inproceedings { dugan-etal-2026-building , title = " Building Auditable {AI} Text Detectors with Sparse Autoencoders " , author = " Dugan, Liam and McDougall, Callum Stuart and Denton, Matthew and Pham, Philip and Kaeser-Chen, Christine and Callison-Burch, Chris " , booktitle = " Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing " , month = oct, year = " 2026 " , address = " Budapest, Hungary " , publisher = " Association for Computational Linguistics " , url = " https://aclanthology.org/2026.emnlp-main.762/ " , pages = " 17640--17689 " , ISBN = " 979-8-89176-459-0 " , } Acknowledgements This research was developed with funding from the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency's (DARPA) SciFy program (Agreement No. HR00112520300) and is based upon work supported in part by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), Intelligence Advanced Research Projects Activity (IARPA), via 56000026C0019 (the BENGAL program).
